title: Statistics
intro:
One short card per topic: a question, the methods, when to use them, and the next question.
Read the card for today's focus before the notebook. All tests on one page: [stats tests cheat sheet](#cheat-stats-tests).

sections.title: Case framework
sections.summary: How to answer any open product or experiment question
sections.body:
**Question:** "Orders fell 10% this week. What do you do?" You have 30 minutes and no clear start.

- **1. Clarify:** which orders, compared to what, since when? Ask before you guess.
- **2. Metric:** pick one main number (orders per day) and a few safety numbers (refunds, app crashes).
- **3. Ideas:** list 3 to 5 possible causes (data bug, holiday, new app version, price change).
- **4. Check:** say which data or test tells the ideas apart (split by platform, run an A/B test).
- **5. Decide:** give a clear answer and what would change your mind.

**Use:** for every open question in the interview. Say the 5 steps out loud first, then fill them in.
**Watch out:** jumping to a test or a cause before you agree on the metric.
**Next question:** you have the numbers. How do you describe them in one or two numbers? -> [Mean, median, spread](#stats-descriptive)

sections.title: Mean, median, spread
sections.summary: One number that describes a group, and how spread out it is
sections.body:
**Question:** 5 friends earn (in $1,000 a month) 3, 3, 4, 5, 100. How much do these friends earn?

- **Mean = 23:** add everyone, divide by 5. The one friend with 100 affects it a lot: nobody actually earns 23.
- **Median = 4:** the friend in the middle. The 100 does not affect it.
- **Mode = 3:** the most common value. Best for categories (most common shoe size).
- **Spread:** groups 50, 50, 50, 50, 50 and 0, 0, 50, 100, 100 both have mean 50, but the standard deviation (`sd`, the typical distance from the mean) is 0 vs 50. With very big or very small values use the IQR (distance between the 25th and 75th percentile).

**Use:** median when a few values are very big or very small (salaries, house prices); mean when values are similar. Always give a spread next to the center.
**Next question:** a coin is flipped 3 times. What is the chance of at least one head? -> [Probability rules](#stats-probability)

sections.title: Probability rules
sections.summary: At least one, given that, expected number
sections.body:
**Question:** you flip a fair coin 3 times. What is the chance of at least one head?

- **Complement:** "at least one" = 1 minus "none". `1 - 0.5^3 = 0.875`.
- **Independent events:** multiply. Three tails = `0.5 * 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.125`.
- **Given that:** `P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)`. Only count the cases where B happened.
- **Expected value:** the long-run average. One die roll: 3.5. Expected heads in 10 flips: `10 * 0.5 = 5` (you can add expected values, even for events that depend on each other).

**Use:** "at least one" -> complement; "and" with independent events -> multiply; "on average how many" -> add expected values.
**Watch out:** adding probabilities of events that can happen together (0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5 is not a probability).
**Next question:** a test says you are sick. What is the chance you really are? -> [Bayes' theorem](#stats-bayes)

sections.title: Bayes' theorem
sections.summary: Flip a 'given that' using how common something is
sections.body:
**Question:** 1% of people have a disease. The test finds 90% of sick people, but also says "positive" for 10% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you are sick?

- **Count 1,000 people:** 10 are sick -> 9 test positive. 990 are healthy -> 99 test positive.
- **Answer:** sick among positives = `9 / (9 + 99) = 8.3%`. Not 90%.
- **Formula:** `P(sick | pos) = P(pos | sick) * P(sick) / P(pos)`.

**Use:** any time a rare thing is flagged: disease tests, fraud alerts, spam filters. The base rate (how common it is, here 1%) affects the answer a lot.
**Watch out:** confusing P(positive | sick) = 90% with P(sick | positive) = 8.3%.
**Next question:** out of 100 visitors, how many will click, and how much does it vary? -> [Common distributions](#stats-distributions)

sections.title: Common distributions
sections.summary: Which shape fits counts, waiting times and averages
sections.body:
**Question:** 100 visitors, each clicks with chance 10%. How many clicks? And other common situations:

| Situation | Distribution | Example result |
|---|---|---|
| yes/no, one try | Bernoulli | click or not, chance 0.1 |
| number of yes in n tries | Binomial | n = 100, p = 0.1: mean 10, variance 9 |
| tries until the first yes | Geometric | p = 0.1: on average 10 tries |
| count per hour, no fixed n | Poisson | 4 calls/hour: chance of 0 calls = 1.8%; mean = variance = 4 |
| waiting time between events | Exponential | 4 per hour: average wait 15 minutes |
| averages, heights | Normal | 68% within 1 sd, 95% within 2 sd |

**Use:** fixed number of tries -> Binomial; counts with no upper limit -> Poisson; averages of many values -> Normal.
**Next question:** spend per user is very uneven. Can we still trust the average? -> [CLT and standard error](#stats-clt-se)

sections.title: CLT and standard error
sections.summary: How precise is an average?
sections.body:
**Question:** 100 users spend on average $20, with sd $50 (a few spend a lot). How precise is the $20?

- **Standard error (SE):** the typical error of the average. `SE = sd / sqrt(n) = 50 / 10 = 5`.
- **More data:** with 10,000 users, `SE = 50 / 100 = 0.5`. 100 times more users -> 10 times smaller error.
- **Central limit theorem (CLT):** the average of many values follows a normal (bell) shape, even when single values are very uneven. That is why z and t tests work.

**Use:** SE for any average or rate. To halve the error you need 4 times the users.
**Watch out:** sd describes users; SE describes the average. Do not mix them.
**Next question:** how do you report the $20 with its error as a range? -> [Confidence intervals](#stats-confidence-intervals)

sections.title: Confidence intervals
sections.summary: Report a number with a range
sections.body:
**Question:** average spend is $20 with SE 5. Conversion is 100 out of 1,000 users. Give a range for each.

- **Mean:** `20 +/- 1.96 * 5` = $10.2 to $29.8 (95% interval).
- **Rate:** `SE = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) = sqrt(0.1 * 0.9 / 1000) = 0.0095`, so 10% +/- 1.9 points = 8.1% to 11.9%.
- **Bootstrap:** for a median or anything unusual, resample the users with replacement 10,000 times and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

**Use:** always report a range, not just one number. If the range for a difference does not include 0, the difference is significant.
**Watch out:** the meaning is "this method catches the true value 95% of the time", not "95% chance this range is right".
**Next question:** a coin gives 60 heads in 100 flips. Is it unfair, or just luck? -> [Hypothesis tests](#stats-hypothesis-tests)

sections.title: Hypothesis tests and p-values
sections.summary: Is a difference real or just luck?
sections.body:
**Question:** a coin gives 60 heads in 100 flips. Is it unfair?

- **H0 (null hypothesis):** "nothing special", the coin is fair.
- **p-value = 0.057:** if the coin were fair, a result this far from 50 happens 5.7% of the time. `scipy.stats.binomtest(60, 100).pvalue`
- **Decision:** with alpha = 0.05 (the cutoff chosen before), 0.057 > 0.05, so we do not call it unfair.
- **Errors:** Type I = false alarm (say unfair when it is fair; chance = alpha). Type II = miss (say fair when it is unfair). Power = 1 minus the miss rate.

**Use:** p < alpha -> the difference is probably real. p > alpha -> not enough evidence (not proof that there is no difference).
**Watch out:** the p-value is not the chance that H0 is true.
**Next question:** you have two groups of numbers. Which test do you run? -> [Choosing a test](#stats-choosing-a-test)

sections.title: Choosing a test
sections.summary: Which test for which data
sections.body:
**Question:** what are you comparing, and what kind of data is it?

| Compare | Test | Python |
|---|---|---|
| averages of 2 groups | Welch t-test | `ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)` |
| same users before vs after | paired t-test | `ttest_rel(before, after)` |
| 2 groups, very uneven values or ranks | Mann-Whitney | `mannwhitneyu(a, b)` |
| rates of 2 groups (10% vs 11%) | z-test for proportions | `proportions_ztest([x1, x2], [n1, n2])` (statsmodels) |
| categories vs categories | chi-square | `chi2_contingency(table)` |
| averages of 3 or more groups | ANOVA | `f_oneway(a, b, c)` |
| one number vs another number | correlation | `pearsonr(x, y)` or `spearmanr(x, y)` |

**Use:** first ask "number or yes/no?", then "how many groups?", then "same users or different users?". All are in `scipy.stats` unless noted.
**Watch out:** using a normal t-test on before/after data from the same users (use the paired one).
**Next question:** how many users do you need before you start? -> [Power and MDE](#stats-power-mde)

sections.title: Power and MDE
sections.summary: How many users does a test need?
sections.body:
**Question:** conversion is 10%. You want to detect a rise to 11%. How many users per group?

- **MDE (minimum detectable effect):** the smallest change you care about. Here 1 point.
- **Power:** the chance to detect the change if it is real. Usually 80%.
- **Quick rule:** `n = 16 * p * (1 - p) / d^2 = 16 * 0.1 * 0.9 / 0.01^2 = 14,400` per group (exact statsmodels answer: about 14,744).
- **Size of the MDE:** half the MDE (0.5 point) -> 4 times the users.

**Use:** compute n before the test, from the MDE the business cares about, then turn n into days of traffic.
**Watch out:** stopping a test that is too small and calling "no difference" a result.
**Next question:** you have the size. How do you set up the test itself? -> [A/B test design](#stats-ab-design)

sections.title: A/B test design
sections.summary: Set up an experiment you can trust
sections.body:
**Question:** you want to test a new checkout button. What do you decide before starting?

- **Unit:** what is randomized, usually the user (not the page view).
- **Split:** random 50/50 into control (old) and treatment (new).
- **Metrics:** one main metric (purchases per user) and guardrails (safety numbers like refunds, page speed).
- **Size and time:** n from the power calculation; run full weeks (at least 1 to 2) to cover weekdays and weekends.
- **Rule:** write the decision rule before looking at the data.

**Use:** say these 5 points for any "how would you test X?" question.
**Watch out:** changing the metric after you see the results.
**Next question:** the test finished. How do you read the result? -> [A/B test analysis](#stats-ab-analysis)

sections.title: A/B test analysis
sections.summary: Read the result of a finished test
sections.body:
**Question:** control: 1,000 buyers out of 10,000 (10%). Treatment: 1,100 out of 10,000 (11%). Did it work?

- **Check the split first:** are the groups the size you expected? (SRM, next card)
- **Difference:** +1 point, or +10% relative.
- **Test:** z-test for proportions, p = 0.021. `proportions_ztest([1100, 1000], [10000, 10000])`
- **Range:** 95% interval of the difference = +0.15 to +1.85 points. It does not include 0, so it is significant.

**Use:** report the difference, its range and the p-value, then the guardrails, then a decision.
**Watch out:** reporting only "p < 0.05" without how big the change is.
**Next question:** the result looks great. What could make it wrong? -> [A/B pitfalls](#stats-ab-pitfalls)

sections.title: A/B pitfalls
sections.summary: What makes a test result wrong
sections.body:
**Question:** your test result looks great. What could still be wrong?

- **Peeking:** checking every day and stopping at the first p < 0.05. With 10 looks, false alarms rise from 5% to about 20%.
- **SRM (sample ratio mismatch):** you expected 50/50 but got 5,000 vs 5,300. Chi-square p = 0.003, so the split is broken: do not trust the result. `chisquare([5000, 5300])`
- **Many metrics:** 20 metrics at alpha 0.05 -> 64% chance that at least one is "significant" by luck.
- **Novelty:** users click a new thing because it is new; the effect fades after a few weeks.
- **Interference:** users in the two groups affect each other (see network effects).

**Use:** check SRM first, fix the duration in advance, correct for many metrics.
**Next question:** the metric is clicks per page view, but you randomized users. Is the usual test still right? -> [Ratio metrics](#stats-ratio-metrics)

sections.title: Ratio metrics
sections.summary: Metrics like clicks per page view
sections.body:
**Question:** 4 users with (views, clicks): (1, 1), (1, 0), (2, 1), (100, 1). What is the click rate?

- **Ratio of totals:** `3 clicks / 104 views = 2.9%`. The heavy user with 100 views affects it a lot.
- **Average per user:** average of 1, 0, 0.5, 0.01 = 37.8%. A different question (the typical user).
- **Correct SE:** page views of one user are not independent. Use the delta method (a formula for the SE of a ratio) or bootstrap by user, not a simple test on page views.

**Use:** when the thing you count (page views) is not the thing you randomize (users).
**Watch out:** a plain test on page views gives too small an SE and too many false "wins".
**Next question:** spend varies a lot between users, so tests need many users. Can we reduce the noise? -> [CUPED](#stats-cuped)

sections.title: CUPED
sections.summary: Use data from before the test to need fewer users
sections.body:
**Question:** spend per user varies a lot, so the test needs many users. Last month's spend of each user predicts this month's spend well. Can that help?

- **Idea:** remove the part of each user's number that last month already explains. `Y_adj = Y - theta * (X - mean(X))`, with `theta = cov(X, Y) / var(X)` and X = last month.
- **Gain:** the variance is multiplied by `1 - rho^2` (rho = correlation of X and Y). With rho = 0.7, only 51% of the variance stays: about half the users needed.
- **Fair:** X is from before the test, so the treatment cannot change it.

**Use:** for metrics where you have the same metric from before the test (spend, sessions).
**Watch out:** never use a variable measured during the test as X.
**Next question:** you want to account for several factors at once (age, country, past spend). -> [Regression](#stats-regression)

sections.title: Regression
sections.summary: How one number changes with others
sections.body:
**Question:** flats of 50, 100 and 150 m2 cost 100, 200 and 300 (in $1,000). How much does one extra m2 add?

- **Linear regression:** fits `price = a + b * size`. Here b = 2: each m2 adds $2,000.
- **Several factors:** `price = a + b1 * size + b2 * rooms`. b1 is the effect of size when rooms stay the same.
- **In A/B tests:** `y ~ treatment + pre_spend` gives the same effect with a smaller SE (like CUPED).
- **Code:** `statsmodels.formula.api.ols("price ~ size", data=df).fit()`.

**Use:** to measure one factor while keeping others fixed, and to reduce noise in tests.
**Watch out:** a coefficient is not a cause. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together because of summer.
**Next question:** no A/B test was possible: a feature launched in one city only. What did it do? -> [Difference in differences](#stats-causal-did)

sections.title: Difference in differences
sections.summary: Effect of a launch without an A/B test
sections.body:
**Question:** a feature launched in city A only. Orders: city A 100 -> 130, city B (no launch) 100 -> 110. What did the feature do?

- **Before vs after in A:** +30. But some of that would have happened anyway.
- **Same change in B:** +10. That is the "anyway" part.
- **DiD:** `(130 - 100) - (110 - 100) = +20` orders from the feature.

**Use:** a launch in one place or at one time, with a similar place that did not get it.
**Watch out:** it only works if both cities moved the same way before the launch (parallel trends). Plot the weeks before to check.
**Next question:** no similar city exists, and users chose the feature themselves. -> [Matching, RD, IV](#stats-causal-psm-rd-iv)

sections.title: Matching, RD, IV
sections.summary: Other ways to find a cause without an A/B test
sections.body:
**Question:** users who joined premium spend more. Is it because of premium, or were they big spenders anyway?

- **Matching (PSM):** pair each premium user with a non-premium user who looked the same before (same past spend, age). Compare the pairs.
- **Regression discontinuity (RD):** a rule makes a cut, e.g. a score of 700 or more gets a discount. Users at 699 and 700 are almost the same, so compare just around the cutoff.
- **Instrument (IV):** something random that pushes people into the treatment but does not change the outcome by itself, e.g. a random invitation email.

**Use:** matching when you can measure what made people choose; RD when a cutoff rule exists; IV when a random push exists.
**Watch out:** matching cannot fix factors you did not measure (motivation).
**Next question:** before any test, which number tells you a product is doing well? -> [Product metrics](#stats-product-metrics)

sections.title: Product metrics
sections.summary: Choose the numbers that measure success
sections.body:
**Question:** you launch photo sharing in a chat app. How do you know if it is a success?

- **North star:** the one number for long-term value (messages sent per active user per week).
- **Feature metrics:** adoption (share of users who send a photo) and how often they use it.
- **Guardrails:** things that must not get worse (app crashes, unsubscribes, load time).
- **Stickiness:** daily users / monthly users, e.g. `300k / 1M = 30%`.

**Use:** give one main metric, 2 to 3 supporting ones and 2 guardrails. Say why each one.
**Watch out:** vanity metrics (total downloads) that only go up and say nothing about value.
**Next question:** your main metric dropped 10% yesterday. What do you do? -> [Metric drop](#stats-metric-drop)

sections.title: Metric drop
sections.summary: Find why a number went down
sections.body:
**Question:** daily active users fell from 1,000 to 900 (-10%). Why?

- **1. Is it real?** Check logging, data pipelines, time zones, dashboard changes.
- **2. Inside or outside?** Inside: new release, bug, price change. Outside: holiday, competitor, news.
- **3. Split it:** by platform, country, app version, new vs old users. Android 500 -> 400, iOS 500 -> 500: the whole drop is Android.
- **4. Dig in:** what changed on Android? A new version released yesterday is a likely cause.

**Use:** always this order: data check, then context, then split, then cause and fix.
**Watch out:** guessing a cause before checking that the data is correct.
**Next question:** a test shows conversion up but revenue a bit down. Do you launch? -> [Launch decisions](#stats-launch-decisions)

sections.title: Launch decisions
sections.summary: Decide when results are mixed
sections.body:
**Question:** treatment: conversion +2% (significant), revenue per user -1% (not significant), page load time +10%. Launch?

| Main metric | Guardrails | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| up, significant | fine | launch |
| up, significant | one is worse | weigh the trade-off, try to fix it, maybe launch to some users |
| flat | fine | launch only if cheap or needed for other reasons |
| down | any | do not launch |

**Here:** check the range of the revenue change (could it be -5%?), fix the load time, then decide.
**Use:** look at the size of the effect and its range, not just the p-value. Think about long-term costs.
**Watch out:** launching on one significant metric out of 20 (could be luck).
**Next question:** in a ride app, treatment drivers take rides from control drivers. Is the test still fair? -> [Network effects](#stats-network-effects)

sections.title: Network effects
sections.summary: When users in the test affect each other
sections.body:
**Question:** a ride app gives treatment drivers a better tool. They get +10% rides, but they take rides from control drivers. What is the real effect?

- **Problem:** control looks worse because treatment took its rides. Measured +10%; the real effect for all drivers could be near 0.
- **Cluster split:** randomize whole cities or friend groups, not single users.
- **Switchback:** switch a whole city between old and new every hour, then compare the hours.

**Use:** marketplaces (riders and drivers), social apps (friends see each other), shared stock or budgets.
**Watch out:** fewer clusters -> less power. 20 cities is a small sample.
**Next question:** you want to look at the results every day and stop early. Is that allowed? -> [Bayesian and sequential tests](#stats-bayesian-sequential)

sections.title: Bayesian and sequential tests
sections.summary: Look at results early without fooling yourself
sections.body:
**Question:** A: 100 buyers out of 1,000. B: 120 out of 1,000. Your manager asks every day "can we stop?".

- **Peeking problem:** a normal test checked 10 times has about 20% false alarms instead of 5%.
- **Sequential test:** a test built for many looks, with a stricter cutoff at each look (alpha spending).
- **Bayesian:** gives "chance B is better than A". With `Beta(1 + buyers, 1 + non-buyers)` for each group: P(B > A) = 92%.

**Use:** sequential when you must be able to stop early; Bayesian when the business wants "chance B is better".
**Watch out:** Bayesian results also need a stopping rule fixed in advance.
**Next question:** the overall effect is +1%. Is it the same for every user? -> [Heterogeneous effects](#stats-heterogeneous-effects)

sections.title: Heterogeneous effects
sections.summary: Effects that differ between groups of users
sections.body:
**Question:** overall effect +1%. New users (20% of users) +6%, old users (80%) -0.25%. Check: `0.2 * 6 + 0.8 * (-0.25) = +1%`.

- **Split by group:** compute the effect for each group (new vs old, country, platform).
- **Interaction in regression:** `y ~ treatment * new_user`. The `treatment:new_user` term shows if the effect differs.
- **Many groups:** with 10 groups, use a stricter cutoff, e.g. `0.05 / 10 = 0.005` (Bonferroni).

**Use:** to target a launch (only new users) or to find who is hurt.
**Watch out:** looking at many groups and reporting only the one that "worked". Choose the groups before the test.
**Next question:** classic interview puzzles: birthdays, doors, dice. -> [Probability puzzles](#stats-probability-puzzles)

sections.title: Probability puzzles
sections.summary: Classic interview puzzles
sections.body:
**Question:** how many people must be in a room for a 50% chance that two share a birthday?

- **Birthday:** 23 people -> 50.7%. Use the complement: `1 - (365/365 * 364/365 * ... * 343/365)`.
- **Monty Hall:** 3 doors, you pick one, the host opens an empty one. Switching wins 2/3, staying wins 1/3.
- **Wait for a 6:** expected number of die rolls = `1 / (1/6) = 6` (Geometric).
- **Tip:** if stuck, simulate in Python with 100,000 random tries.

**Use:** complement for "at least one", count all cases for "given that", expected value for "on average".
**Next question:** want all tests on one page? -> [Stats tests cheat sheet](#cheat-stats-tests)
